headings: ### Hear the Protective Part First (not in yet)

rows.label: P1 · candidate (alone 100% Human, 90; turn 25)
rows.text: Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. A harder voice can seem more fitting for something that's been in your way. I'd still keep it the same. If that voice isn't there in you yet, borrow it from someone who's been safe for you. At some point you can ask that part, "What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?" It might say this will just be one more performance, and you'll fool yourself again.
guide: Offer it the same Nurturer voice

rows.label: P2 · yours (100% Human, medium on your check)
rows.text: That one can sting, because there could be something to it. Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. "Tell me what you remember, I'm listening." works well here. It puts you into the role of the Nurturer, which alleviates the instinct to argue back. Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo! If you push past it, you might get exactly the performance it was afraid of. Even if you didn't win an Emmy last year, that can look convincing, with the right words and maybe even tears, while nothing underneath feels any safer.
rows.note: Your four changes, each where the AI part began.

rows.label: P3 · round 3 (alone 100% AI)
rows.text: A new roommate doesn't win you over with a speech on move-in day. The rent just has to keep showing up. Your Protector, the grown-up you, earns that protective part's trust about the same way, mostly out in ordinary life. The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.

rows.label: P4 · round 3 (alone 100% AI)
rows.text: You could tell that part, "You can stay right there and watch, and I'll stop if it gets to be too much." Most protective parts can live with a deal like that, and it keeps you to one small step at a time. And if it says no? Then it's no. When it does let you go on, follow whatever changes. A critic that kept saying "This is stupid" might soften into "I'm scared to get my hopes up." That one's easier to be kind to.

rows.label: P5 · round 3, shortened (alone 100% AI)
rows.text: No need to restart the whole exercise and go looking for your little one again, like they're hiding behind the couch. Maybe a vague hurt turns out to be about wanting someone on your side for once. Oof. If it does, try being that someone. You could even say it out loud: "I'm on your side." It may feel silly to say out loud. Notice how it lands anyway. Sometimes all that happens is your shoulders come down a little.
